To adjourn means to officially bring a formal gathering — such as a court session, a parliamentary debate, or a business meeting — to a close, either temporarily or permanently. The key idea is that this closing is deliberate and declared. A session doesn't simply "end" — it is adjourned by someone with the authority to do so.
Temporary vs. permanent — the most important nuance

When something is adjourned, it can go one of two ways:

Temporarily — The session is paused with a plan to continue later, at a specific time or date. "The judge adjourned the trial until next Thursday." This means the proceedings aren't over for good; they'll resume at the stated time.

Indefinitely (or permanently) — Sometimes a session is adjourned with no future date set. In formal contexts this is called adjourning sine die, meaning the session is simply over with nothing scheduled. Parliaments are often adjourned this way at the end of a legislative term.
A second meaning: adjourning to somewhere

There's an older, less formal use of adjourn that you may come across. When a formal gathering ends, the participants sometimes move together as a group to another location, and this movement can also be described as "adjourning to" that place.

"After the board meeting, the executives adjourned to the dining room for dinner."

Here it simply means they finished formal business and relocated as a group. This usage is more common in older or British writing, but you'll still encounter it.
How adjourn differs from similar words

This is important, because several words are close in meaning but are not the same.

Adjourn vs. Recess — A recess is a short pause within an ongoing session. A court might break for lunch and return an hour later; the session itself is still alive. An adjournment formally ends the session (even if a new session starts the next day). Think of recess as pressing pause, and adjournment as pressing stop.

Adjourn vs. Postpone — To postpone means to delay the start of something that hasn't happened yet. You postpone a meeting before it begins. You adjourn a meeting that is already in progress. Postpone points to the future; adjourn deals with something currently happening.

Adjourn vs. Cancel — Cancelling means something won't happen or is dropped entirely. Adjourning is a formal, structured close — it doesn't necessarily mean the matter is abandoned. A case can be adjourned and then resumed; a cancelled meeting is simply gone.

Adjourn vs. Suspend — Suspending proceedings often implies something unexpected interrupted the session, or that normal rules are being set aside for a reason. Adjournment is typically a routine, planned act of formally closing a session in the normal course of business.

Not everyone has the power to adjourn. In most formal settings, only the presiding officer — the judge, the chairperson, the speaker of a parliament — can declare a session adjourned. Sometimes the group itself can vote to adjourn.

The word is most at home in these settings: courts of law (judges adjourn hearings and trials), parliaments and legislatures (sessions are adjourned by the speaker or by vote), board and committee meetings (the chairperson adjourns once business is complete), and formal conferences (delegations adjourn international sessions).
The word in its different forms

• She adjourns the meeting. — present tense
  • The court was adjourned. — past tense; this passive form is the most common in everyday writing, because attention is on the meeting, not on who adjourned it
  • They are adjourning. — present continuous
  • The adjournment lasted two days. — noun form
  • After adjourning, the members left. — gerund (the -ing form used as a noun or describing an action)
A simple mental image to lock it in

Picture a judge in a courtroom. Everything is formal, structured, and official. When business is done — or needs to pause — the judge strikes a gavel and says: "Court adjourned." That single act is the formal declaration that what was officially opened is now officially closed, even if only for the day. That gavel strike is the essence of adjourn: a deliberate, authorized act of bringing a formal session to its conclusion.
